objectives: Reason about critical minerals + supply chains.

slides.title: Ore deposits: how Earth concentrates metals
slides.body:
**Ore**: rock with sufficient concentration of valuable element to be economic.

**Crustal averages vs ore grades**:
- Iron: 5% in crust; ore typically 30-65%. Concentration factor ~10×.
- Copper: 50 ppm in crust; ore 0.5-2%. ~100-400×.
- Gold: 4 ppb in crust; ore 1-5 ppm. ~1000×.
- Platinum: 5 ppb; ore 5-15 ppm. ~1000-3000×.
- Lithium: 20 ppm; ore 1-2% in pegmatites or ~2000 ppm in brines.

**Major ore-deposit types** (genetic classification):

**Magmatic** (within or from igneous):
- **Layered mafic intrusions**: gravity settling concentrates dense minerals. Bushveld (S Africa) — world's largest platinum + chromium; Sudbury (Canada) — Ni-Cu-PGE.
- **Kimberlite pipes**: from deep mantle. Diamonds. Africa, Russia, Canada, Australia.
- **Carbonatites**: rare alkaline magmas. REEs, niobium. Mountain Pass (USA), Mount Weld (Australia), Bayan Obo (China).

**Hydrothermal** (hot-fluid concentration):
- **Porphyry copper**: large, low-grade Cu-Mo deposits. Chile, Peru, USA (Bingham, Morenci), Indonesia. Most of world's copper.
- **Epithermal gold**: shallow + hot-spring deposits. Nevada (Carlin trend), Indonesia (Grasberg), Peru (Yanacocha).
- **Skarns**: at contact between intrusions + carbonate. W, Cu, Zn, Au.
- **VMS (Volcanogenic Massive Sulfide)**: at submarine hydrothermal vents. Pb, Zn, Cu, Ag.
- **SEDEX (Sedimentary Exhalative)**: hydrothermal in sedimentary basins. Pb, Zn (McArthur River, Australia).
- **MVT (Mississippi Valley-type)**: low-temperature carbonate-hosted. Pb, Zn (Tri-State district USA).

**Sedimentary**:
- **BIF (Banded Iron Formations)**: Precambrian. Most of world's iron ore. Brazil, Australia, USA, China.
- **Phosphorites**: marine phosphate deposits. Morocco, China, USA.
- **Placer deposits**: gold, diamonds, tin, REEs concentrated in stream beds + beaches. Witwatersrand (S Africa) — world's largest gold deposit, ~50% of all gold ever mined.
- **Evaporites**: halite, potash, lithium. Salar de Atacama (Chile, Li), Salar de Uyuni (Bolivia, Li), Saskatchewan (potash).

**Weathering / supergene**:
- **Bauxite**: weathered Al-rich rocks → aluminum ore. Australia, Guinea, Brazil.
- **Lateritic Ni**: weathered ultramafic → nickel. Indonesia, Philippines, New Caledonia.
- **Supergene copper**: weathering enriches porphyry copper deposits.

**Coal**: from buried plants. Carboniferous (USA Appalachia, Europe), Permian (Australia, S Africa, India, USA Powder River).

**Petroleum + gas**: from buried marine + lake organic matter.

**Aggregate** (sand + gravel): glacial + fluvial deposits. Essential for construction + most-mined material by volume.

slides.title: Critical minerals + the 21st-century supply chain
slides.body:
**Critical minerals**: essential to economy + national security, with supply risk.

**US Geological Survey 2022 Critical Minerals List** (50 minerals):
- Aluminum, antimony, arsenic, barite, beryllium, bismuth, cesium, chromium, cobalt, dysprosium, erbium, europium, fluorspar, gadolinium, gallium, germanium, graphite, hafnium, holmium, indium, iridium, lanthanum, lithium, lutetium, magnesium, manganese, neodymium, nickel, niobium, palladium, platinum, praseodymium, rhodium, rubidium, ruthenium, samarium, scandium, tantalum, tellurium, terbium, thulium, tin, titanium, tungsten, vanadium, ytterbium, yttrium, zinc, zirconium.

**EU Critical Raw Materials Act 2024**: 34 strategic + critical raw materials. Targets domestic production + recycling + import diversification.

**Battery minerals** (the EV transition):
- **Lithium**: cathodes + electrolyte. Chile, Australia, Argentina (the 'lithium triangle'); China processes ~60% of refined Li.
- **Cobalt**: cathodes. DRC produces ~70%; child labor + ethical concerns.
- **Nickel**: high-energy-density cathodes. Indonesia (Class 1 from laterites), Russia, Philippines.
- **Manganese**: cathodes + steel. S Africa, Gabon, Australia.
- **Graphite**: anodes. China dominates synthetic + natural.

**Rare Earth Elements (REEs)**:
- 15 lanthanides + Y + Sc.
- 'Critical' uses: permanent magnets (Nd, Pr, Dy, Tb) for EVs + wind turbines; phosphors (Eu, Tb, Y); catalysts (Ce, La); lasers (Nd, Er, Ho).
- China dominates: ~60% of mine production + ~85% of processing.
- Largest deposit: Bayan Obo (China). USA Mountain Pass (CA, MP Materials) restarted.
- Geopolitically sensitive — China has used REE supply as leverage (2010 Senkaku Islands dispute).

**Semiconductor critical**:
- Silicon (abundant).
- Germanium, gallium: GaN/SiC for power electronics. China major producer.
- Indium, tellurium, selenium: thin-film solar.

**Supply-chain dynamics**:
- Mineral exploration: 7-15 years from discovery to production.
- Processing dominance: China processes ~50-80% of many critical minerals (regardless of mine location).
- Substitution: research into alternative materials (LFP batteries reduce Co + Ni dependence).
- Recycling: growing but still small fraction of supply.

**Geopolitics of resources**:
- DRC + cobalt: ethical + supply concerns.
- China + REEs + processing: technology + national-security implications.
- USA + Inflation Reduction Act 2022: tax credits for domestic + 'free trade agreement' country sourcing.
- Critical Minerals Partnership (USA + allies).
- Mining + indigenous land rights tensions.

**Future of mining**:
- Mining lower grades (depletion of high-grade deposits).
- Deeper underground.
- Tailings reprocessing.
- Deep-sea mining (controversial; Clarion-Clipperton Zone in Pacific has polymetallic nodules with Ni, Cu, Co, Mn).
- Asteroid mining (speculative).
- Bioleaching + improved metallurgy.

slides.title: Petroleum + groundwater + sustainability + the geological view
slides.body:
**Petroleum geology**:
- Source rock → migration → reservoir → trap.
- Conventional vs unconventional.
- Exploration tools: seismic reflection (modern 3D + 4D), gravity, magnetics, geochemistry, well logs.
- Drilling: vertical → horizontal → multi-stage fracking.

**Major hydrocarbon-producing regions**:
- Middle East: Saudi Arabia (Ghawar — largest field), UAE, Iran, Iraq, Kuwait.
- USA: Permian basin (TX/NM), Bakken (ND), Marcellus (PA/WV/OH), Eagle Ford (TX), Haynesville.
- Russia: West Siberia, East Siberia, Caspian.
- N Sea (declining): UK + Norway.
- Brazil pre-salt (Santos, Campos basins) — deep offshore.
- West Africa (Angola, Nigeria).
- Canada oil sands (Athabasca).

**Peak oil**: idea that production peaks then declines. Multiple revised forecasts; shale revolution delayed USA peak. Global peak demand likely before peak supply due to EV/renewable transition.

**Stranded assets**: fossil-fuel reserves that may not be developed due to climate policy + market shifts. Trillions of dollars potentially.

**Groundwater + aquifers**:
- ~30% of global freshwater is groundwater.
- Major aquifers: Ogallala (US Great Plains, depleting), Guarani (S America), N Sahara, N China Plain.
- Recharge often slow (centuries-millennia for confined aquifers).
- Overpumping: land subsidence (Mexico City, Bangkok, Jakarta), saltwater intrusion (coastal), aquifer collapse.

**Water resources are increasingly stressed by**:
- Population growth + agricultural demand.
- Climate change (altered precipitation patterns).
- Pollution (PFAS, nitrate, pesticides, industrial).

**Carbon storage in geology**:
- Saline aquifers: largest capacity.
- Depleted oil + gas reservoirs: well-characterized.
- Basalt mineralization: CO₂ reacts with basalt to form stable carbonates (CarbFix in Iceland).
- Unmineable coal seams + CBM stimulation.
- Active commercial CCS: ~40 projects globally; scaling rapidly.

**Geothermal energy**:
- Conventional: in volcanic regions (Iceland, NZ, USA, Indonesia, Kenya).
- Enhanced geothermal systems (EGS): drill anywhere with sufficient heat. Fervo Energy 2023 breakthrough.

**Sustainability + circular economy**:
- Recycling: aluminum + steel highly recycled; battery materials growing; rare earths challenging.
- Substitution: research into less-critical materials.
- Mining efficiency: deeper, lower-grade requires more energy.
- ESG (Environmental, Social, Governance) standards for mining.
- Indigenous rights + free-prior-informed consent (FPIC) standards.

**Geology + civilization**:
- Every modern technology depends on geological resources.
- Energy transition requires VAST minerals: estimated 4-6× current mining for net-zero by 2050.
- Trade-off: more mining for clean energy vs reduced fossil-fuel mining.
- 'No raw materials, no transition'.
- Geologists, geophysicists, mining engineers + critical-minerals strategy increasingly important in 21st century.

**Modern frontiers**:
- ML-augmented mineral exploration (KoBold Metals, GoldSpot).
- Hyperspectral satellite imaging for surface mineralogy.
- Drone-based geophysics.
- In-situ leaching for low-grade ores.
- Bioleaching.
- 'Smart' mining with autonomous trucks + AI control.

question.question: Lithium supply for EVs
question.goal: An EV battery requires ~10 kg Li. World EV production target: 80M EVs/year by 2030. Compute Li demand vs current production.

steps.reveal: 800,000 tons (800 kt) Li per year just for EVs.

steps.prompt: Current world Li production (2024): ~180,000 tons. Gap?
steps.reveal: ~4-5× current production. Massive expansion needed by 2030.

steps.prompt: Where will new supply come from?

options: Existing producers (Chile, Australia, Argentina, China) ramp. New: brine projects in lithium triangle, new spodumene mines, USA (Thacker Pass), Africa (DRC, Zimbabwe, Mali), DLE (direct lithium extraction) from geothermal brines (Salton Sea CA). Plus: recycling (small now but growing) + substitution (LFP, sodium-ion batteries reduce per-vehicle Li need).

steps.reveal: Ramping existing producers + new mines + DLE + recycling + chemistry substitution. All scaling fast. Bottleneck: capital, permitting, ESG concerns + processing (China dominates). Geopolitics of Li transition is major 2020s story.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{Li for EVs: 4-5x current production needed by 2030; supply scaling rapidly}}$$ The energy transition is also a MINING transition. Vast quantities of Li, Ni, Co, Cu, REEs, Mn, graphite needed. Mining + processing + supply-chain are 21st century geopolitical + economic flashpoints. Geologists + mineral exploration + ESG-aware mining + processing capacity + recycling all critical. The geological view of the energy transition: enabling resources, supply-chain risks, environmental + social trade-offs.

question.question: China dominates ~60% of rare earth element MINING + ~85% of PROCESSING. Why both?
options: Mining: China has massive Bayan Obo deposit (carbonatite) discovered + developed early. Processing: chemistry + refining requires capital + tech + environmental tolerance (REEs need separation via solvent extraction, generates radioactive thorium waste). China invested + accepted environmental costs; Western processing largely shut down due to costs + environmental regulations. Now reshoring (USA Mountain Pass, etc.) but takes years.
question.explanation:
Rare earth supply chain dominance has two components:

**Mining**: ~60% China. Bayan Obo (Inner Mongolia) is largest single REE deposit. China developed it heavily 1980s-2000s. Other deposits exist (Mountain Pass USA, Mt. Weld Australia, Lynas Malaysia processing) but China's been the production leader. Demand outstripped Western supply through 1990s-2010s.

**Processing**: ~85% China. Even REE concentrate from non-Chinese mines often sent to China for separation. Why:
- Separating individual rare earths from concentrate requires hundreds of solvent-extraction stages. Capital-intensive.
- Generates radioactive thorium waste (rare earths co-occur with Th + U in carbonatites).
- Environmental + regulatory costs high in West.
- China accepted environmental costs + invested in expertise.

Result: even if you mine REEs in USA or Australia, you'd ship concentrate to China for refining. Strategic vulnerability.

Reshoring efforts:
- **MP Materials (Mountain Pass)** restarting Stage III processing in USA (2024+).
- **Lynas (Australia + Malaysia)** processing.
- **Western Australia Iluka Resources** new processing facility.
- **EU Critical Raw Materials Act** + USA Inflation Reduction Act incentives.
- Takes 5-15 years to develop full processing capacity.

2010 Senkaku Islands dispute: China briefly restricted REE exports to Japan; demonstrated leverage. Drove diversification efforts.

slides.workedSolution: China has both mining (Bayan Obo) + processing dominance. Processing is capital-intensive + environmentally challenging; West shut down; China accepted costs. Even non-Chinese mined REEs often refined in China. Reshoring: MP Materials, Lynas, EU CRM Act, USA IRA. Takes years; ongoing strategic effort.

question.question: Copper porphyry deposit: 0.5% Cu over 1 km³. Tons of contained Cu (assume density 2.5 t/m³)?
Deep-sea polymetallic nodules
question.prompt: Clarion-Clipperton Zone in Pacific has vast polymetallic nodules with Ni, Cu, Co, Mn. International Seabed Authority debating mining. Walk through pros + cons.
Explain in two or three sentences why economic geology is critical to the 21st-century energy + technology transitions.
question.rubric: Mentions that the green transition requires vast amounts of critical minerals (Li, Co, Ni, Cu, REEs, etc.); mineral exploration + extraction + processing + recycling are bottlenecks; geopolitics of supply (China dominance in many; DRC for cobalt; few alternative sources) drives industrial + diplomatic strategy; geology underpins both fossil-fuel + renewable-energy economies + ESG considerations now front + center in mining.
